questions.q: What does 'using a model as-is' mean?
options: Calling a model that someone has already fine-tuned for your exact task, without any further training of your own
Training a model from randomly initialized weights
Deleting the model's tokenizer
Running a model without ever loading its weights
questions.explain: As-is usage means trusting an existing fine-tune — lesson 23's sentiment-analysis pipeline, already fine-tuned on SST-2, is a working example.

questions.q: What is the key difference between fine-tuning and training a model from scratch?
options: Fine-tuning never uses backpropagation
Fine-tuning requires no labeled data at all
Fine-tuning can only be done on images, never text
Fine-tuning starts from a pretrained model's existing weights instead of random ones, then continues training on your own data
questions.explain: Fine-tuning uses the same backpropagation and gradient descent as training from scratch, but starts from weights that already encode general language understanding.

questions.q: Why does fine-tuning typically use a much smaller learning rate than training a model from scratch?
options: Smaller learning rates train faster in every case
It has no effect on the outcome
A large learning rate during fine-tuning can overwrite what the model already learned during pretraining — a failure mode called catastrophic forgetting
The Trainer API requires it as a hard rule
questions.explain: A small learning rate nudges the pretrained weights toward the new task without erasing the general knowledge they already encode.

questions.q: What does the Hugging Face Hub's 'Finetuned from' field on a model card show?
options: The model's exact accuracy score
A link back to the specific base model this one was fine-tuned from, plus a list of other models finetuned from the same base
The number of GPUs used during training
A random, unrelated model recommendation
questions.explain: The lesson's screenshot showed this real Hub feature: a model card that declares its base model and links to both that base model's page and other finetunes of it.

questions.q: According to the lesson, if a model already fine-tuned for your exact task exists and scores well, what's the recommended approach?
options: Always fine-tune it further anyway, just in case
Ignore it and train a new model from scratch
Delete your own labeled data
Use it as-is — fine-tuning it again on a small dataset of your own could make it worse by overfitting
questions.explain: The lesson's decision table recommends using an existing, well-performing fine-tune as-is, since retraining it on a tiny dataset risks overfitting rather than improving it.
